newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Exchange Fund bills spread widens as RTGS looms.
newsitem.headline: HK Exchange Fund bills spread widens as RTGS looms.

text.p: The spread between Hong Kong Exchange Fund bill yields and the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) widened sharply on Thursday, causing a huge increase in banks' settlement costs, traders said.
The spread widened to 120-150 basis points, making the cost of holding paper for the upcoming Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system extremely high, money market dealers said.
"If banks buy short-term bills and at the same time run match funding then they have to pay 120 basis points a day," a Japanese bank dealer said.
RTGS will formally start operations on Monday although banks have been using the system in a simulation test since November.
One-month Exchange Fund bills yielded 4.25 percent or 149 basis points below one-month HIBOR, which settled at 5.74432 percent.
Pressure on government paper yields started as banks began accumulating the paper in anticipation of the RTGS launch.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has said that banks can use Exchange Fund bills and notes to obtain interest-free intraday liquidity by carrying out intraday repurchase transactions with the HKMA under the RTGS system.

But dealers said the cost of carrying government paper has increased banks' operating costs because of the large gap between the yield on Exchange Fund instruments and interbank rates, which represents the banks' borrowing costs.
They said this effect was especially evident for foreign banks, many of which have limited retail business in Hong Kong.
"Foreign banks' retail deposit base is relatively small and they mainly rely on the interbank market for liquidity and that will be much more expensive (for them)," a dealer said.
The current spread of more than one percent on bills is exceptional compared with the 30-40 basis points in the local market earlier this year, a European bank dealer said.
He added that the Hong Kong spread also compares poorly with that between short-dated U.S. Treasuries and U.S. interbank rates, which is below 30 basis points.
Dealers said the widening in the spread has been exacerbated because some banks put off buying government paper as long as possible, causing steep falls on bill yields on Thursday.
"The sharp fall on bill yields is partly because some banks are waiting for the very last minute to buy," the European bank dealer said.
Dealers said they feared the spread would widen further as banks come out for a last round of bills buying on Friday.

Traders now preferred to buy bills with maturities of one month or less as the risk for holding short-dated paper would be relatively small if the market dumps paper after traders become more familiar with RTGS and find they do not need to hold so much, one dealer said.
In response to the strong demand for short-dated bills, the HKMA has issued three special 28-day bills totalling HK$20 billion in the past two weeks to ease tightness.
The authority also injected more than HK$3.0 billion, before extracting about half of it, into the interbank market to bring down short-term rates.
"HKMA did give some help but I believe it may take several months for the market to return to normal," the European bank dealer said.
